theme: False teachers; the day of the Lord
readingInstruction: Read 2 Peter 2:1-3:18. The first chapter warns against false teachers, and the second looks ahead to the day of the Lord. Notice Peter’s use of Old Testament examples and his answer to the scoffers who ask, “Where is the promise of his coming?”
settingTheScene: Peter’s readers were threatened by false teachers who were morally lax and who mocked the idea that Christ would return. Peter’s response is stern about the teachers (chapter 2) and pastoral toward the believers (chapter 3). The letter has many similarities to Jude, and many scholars think Peter and Jude drew on a common warning. The second chapter is among the strongest descriptions of false teaching in the Bible.
observation: “There will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies” (2:1).
“Then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials” (2:9).
“Scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing” (3:3).
“Where is the promise of his coming?” (3:4).
“With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (3:8).
“The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (3:9).
“According to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (3:13).
“But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).
interpretation:
Peter says that just as false prophets arose in Israel, “there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.” They are known by their doctrine and their lives: many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. They exploit others with false words. But judgment is certain. Peter gives three examples: the angels who sinned and were cast into hell, the ancient world destroyed by the flood (with Noah preserved as a herald of righteousness), and Sodom and Gomorrah (with Lot rescued). “Then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment.” God both saves and judges.

The false teachers are described vividly: following the flesh in corrupt desire, despising authority, bold and willful, “like irrational animals.” They are “springs without water and mists driven by a storm.” They promise freedom, “but they themselves are slaves of corruption.” Peter says it would have been better never to have known the way of righteousness than to turn back from it, as a dog returns to its vomit and a washed sow to wallowing in the mire.

Chapter 3 begins with a reminder. Peter writes to stir up their sincere minds to remember the words of the prophets and the apostles. “Knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation.” Peter answers: they forget that God created the world by his word, and that the same word destroyed the world by water and now holds the present heavens and earth for fire. Delay is not slowness. “With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.” God is not bound by our clock. “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” Delay is mercy. Christians who hold to unconditional election read “you” as the elect, God’s people, for whom he waits until all are gathered. Others read “all” broadly as God’s desire for every person. Either way, patience calls for repentance.

“But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the elements will be dissolved with heat, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.” Interpreters debate whether this means the complete destruction of the present creation or its purging and renewal by fire, as metal is refined. Many hold the latter, noting the comparison to Noah’s flood, which did not annihilate the earth. The end result is clear: “According to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.”

So what kind of people should we be? “Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God?” Be diligent to be found without spot or blemish, at peace. Beware of being carried away with the error of lawless people. And the closing charge: “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.”
connection: Jude 4-19 closely parallels chapter 2. Genesis 6-8 and 19 record the flood and Sodom. Numbers 22-24 tells the story of Balaam. Proverbs 26:11 is quoted in 2:22. Psalm 90:4 stands behind 3:8. Matthew 24:36-44 and 1 Thessalonians 5:2 describe the Lord coming like a thief. Habakkuk 2:3 speaks of waiting for a delayed vision. Romans 2:4 says God’s kindness leads to repentance. 1 Timothy 2:4 says God desires all to be saved. Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 promise new heavens and a new earth. Romans 8:19-23 and Revelation 21:1-5 describe the renewed creation.
application:
Test the teaching you hear against Scripture. Ask where it comes from, what it says about Christ, and what kind of lives its teachers lead.

Reframe a delay in your own life, such as an unanswered prayer or a waiting season, in light of 3:8-9. How might God be showing patience?

Pick one way to “grow in grace and knowledge” this week, such as a book of the Bible or a theological book.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from false teachers.
Thank him that he knows how to rescue the godly.
Ask him to help you grow in grace and in knowledge of Jesus.
